fieldNotes.listing.powertrain: Resolved from the VIN via NHTSA vPIC, never from the model name — a "Hyundai Ioniq" is sold as a hybrid, a plug-in hybrid AND a battery EV. `vinVerified: false` means range/energy/battery figures are model-level assumptions; a `caution` string is then present.
fieldNotes.listing.electricDriveShare: Fraction of miles actually driven on electricity at 130 mi/week (~19 mi/day). 1 = battery-electric. A plug-in hybrid with ~50 miles of range approaches 1 at this duty cycle, i.e. it runs as a de-facto EV; a short-range plug-in does not. This is the meaningful measure of "primarily electric drive", not battery presence.
fieldNotes.listing.safety.*.confidence: "vin-trim-confirmed" = the manufacturer reports this as standard for this VIN's trim (NHTSA vPIC). "model-year-typical" = model-year research, NOT confirmed for this car. "unknown" = no data. vPIC is a paperwork record, not a physical inspection — confirm on the vehicle.
fieldNotes.listing.safety.*.equipped: true only when confirmed standard. null means unconfirmed, which is NOT the same as absent — many manufacturers simply do not submit this field (Toyota reports blind-spot for 0 of its listings here).
fieldNotes.listing.safety.iihsAward: IIHS does not test every powertrain variant of a model. An award applies to the variant named in it, which may differ from this car; iihsNotRatedNote flags that case.
fieldNotes.listing.battery.riskFactor: 0 = no modelled degradation/replacement exposure; higher = more. Feeds the batteryAllowance line in costToOwn.
fieldNotes.listing.battery.federalWarranty: US federal minimum is 8 years / 100,000 miles on the traction battery, transferable to subsequent owners. Some states and manufacturers exceed it.
fieldNotes.reliabilityByModelYear.*.band: clean | ok | watch | concern | unknown — a qualitative band, NOT a numeric score. Scope is the model-year, so it says nothing about the condition of an individual car. Get a pre-purchase inspection. `unknown` with recordRetrieved:false means the NHTSA lookup found no matching model — ABSENCE OF DATA, never a clean record.
fieldNotes.reliabilityByModelYear.*.queriedAsNhtsaM: The model name actually queried. NHTSA matches names exactly and splits many models by powertrain variant ("IONIQ HYBRID" vs "IONIQ PLUG-IN HYBRID" vs "IONIQ ELECTRIC"; "CLARITY PLUG-IN HYBRID" vs "CLARITY FUEL CELL"), returning an empty result with HTTP 200 on a miss. The variant is chosen from the VIN-resolved powertrain, never by name similarity. This field lets you verify we asked about the right car.
fieldNotes.reliabilityByModelYear.*.sourceUrl: Triangulated from freely accessible public sources, primarily NHTSA complaints/recalls. NOT J.D. Power and NOT Consumer Reports. Complaint counts are not adjusted for sales volume, so raw counts are not comparable between a high-volume and a low-volume model.
fieldNotes.listing.vehicleHistory: From the dealer-supplied CARFAX/AutoCheck summary on the listing. Badges come in affirming/negating pairs, so true AND false are both affirmative statements from the report; null means NEITHER badge was present, i.e. NOT REPORTED. Never read null as the negative. Always pull a full VIN history before buying.
fieldNotes.listing.costToOwn: totalCostOfOwnership = purchasePrice + salesTax + fuelAndElectricity + maintenance + insurance + registrationAndFees + majorRepairReserve − resaleValueRecovered. Inputs are in costAssumptions.
fieldNotes.listing.repairOutlook: ONE framework applied to every powertrain. Each hazard attaches only to components that powertrain actually has — an EV carries no engine, transmission, exhaust or emissions hazard; a plug-in hybrid carries BOTH the engine set and the high-voltage set. expectedReserveUsd is Σ(probability × cost) and is the budget number, already included in costToOwn.*.costs.majorRepairReserve; worstCaseExposure is the single largest plausible bill and is deliberately NOT averaged into it. Probabilities are engineering estimates scaled by age, odometer and ownership length, with stated ranges — not actuarial data. See repairHazardCatalog for each hazard's cost range and basis. NOTE: an earlier version of this model charged electric cars a battery allowance and charged gasoline and hybrid cars nothing for major repairs, which biased every cost comparison against EVs; correcting it moved electric cars up roughly 24 ranking places on average.
fieldNotes.listing.batteryHealth: Capacity loss ONLY. It reduces range and resale value and is deliberately NOT charged as a repair; catastrophic pack failure is a separate hazard in repairOutlook. Projected from pack age, odometer and thermal-management type for Seattle's mild climate and mostly overnight AC home charging — the two conditions that most slow degradation. Heat and frequent DC fast charging are the main accelerators and neither is expected here. This is a projection, not a measurement: verify with a real state-of-health readout (LeafSpy or equivalent) before buying.
fieldNotes.listing.viability2032: Coarse judgement of whether the car is still economically worth owning at the end of the 6-year window, from age, mileage, projected battery health, and the size of the expected repair reserve relative to the car's value. Condition of the individual car dominates all of it — get a pre-purchase inspection.
fieldNotes.repairHazardCatalog: Definitions for the hazard ids referenced by listing.repairOutlook.components, stated once here rather than repeated on every car. Includes the cost range and the basis for each probability.
fieldNotes.listing.ranking.matchScore: Internal 0-100 fit score used to order the page: safety, then cost to own, then longevity, multiplied by reliability and title-history factors. Powertrain-neutral by design — electric cars are not given a bonus, so where they win they win on cost. Not a quality rating.
fieldNotes.listing.stillListed: false means the car was in a previous scan but the latest one no longer returns it — probably sold.

shortlists.note: Two rankings on purpose. topOverall is powertrain-neutral. topElectric applies the stated preference for primarily-electric driving, kept as a separate list so the bias is visible rather than hidden inside matchScore.

topElectric.note: Battery-electric and plug-in hybrids only, VIN-verified, ranked by overall fit — NOT by electric share. Ranking by share alone would put every 100%-electric BEV above every plug-in and hide the fact that a 53-mile Volt covers ~85% of these miles on electricity while costing several thousand less to own. Read electricDriveShare alongside the rank.

suspension-brakes.basis: Engineering estimate. Struts, bushings, wheel bearings and calipers on a decade-old car. Regenerative braking meaningfully extends pad and rotor life on hybrids and EVs, so the low end of the range applies to them.

ev-drive-unit.component: Drive unit, inverter or onboard charger
ev-drive-unit.basis: Engineering estimate. The electric drivetrain has one moving part and an excellent field record; the money risk sits in power electronics and the onboard charger rather than the motor.

ev-battery-failure.basis: Recurrent Auto's fleet analysis puts out-of-warranty battery REPLACEMENT at roughly 1.5% of all EVs, and well under 1% for 2016-and-newer model years, once recall campaigns are excluded. Widened here to account for out-of-warranty repair on cheap older cars and for the fact that a used or refurbished pack — not a $16,000 dealer pack — is the realistic remedy at this price point. This is FAILURE ONLY; gradual capacity loss is handled in batteryHealth().

hv-thermal-hvac.basis: Engineering estimate. Electric compressors and coolant heaters are a known EV maintenance item. Passively-cooled packs skip this hardware entirely, which is why they are cheaper to fix and worse at surviving heat.

transmission.basis: Engineering estimate. The single most expensive common failure on a high-mileage conventional automatic or CVT. Deliberately NOT applied to hybrids: Toyota/Hyundai/Kia hybrids use a planetary eCVT with no clutch packs or torque converter, which is a genuinely different and more durable device.

cooling-fuel.basis: Engineering estimate. Water pumps, radiators, thermostats, fuel pumps, coil packs — individually modest, collectively near-certain across six years on a car of this age.

emissions.basis: Engineering estimate, informed by the high rate of P0420-type emissions faults on 10+ year old cars and by catalytic-converter theft rates in the Puget Sound region. Required to pass Washington emissions and to sell the car.

engine.basis: Engineering estimate. Catastrophic engine failure is uncommon on the Japanese/Korean 4-cylinders in this roster; the risk is concentrated in neglected examples, which is why a service history matters more than the average.

starter-alternator.basis: Engineering estimate. Full hybrids and EVs have neither component — hybrids start the engine with the traction motor and charge the 12 V system from the high-voltage pack.

hybrid-battery.basis: Engineering estimate. Full-hybrid packs are small and a healthy aftermarket exists, so this is a real but bounded bill rather than a write-off. Rises steeply past ~150,000 miles.

costAssumptions.note: These are the INPUTS to every costToOwn figure. Change one and every total moves.
knownWeaknesses: Insurance is the single largest line item over six years and is an ESTIMATE. It has not been checked against a real teen-driver quote.
NHTSA complaint counts are not adjusted for sales volume, so raw counts are not comparable between a high-volume and a low-volume model.
Washington's used-EV sales-tax exemption appears to have lapsed 2025-07-31 and is deliberately NOT modelled.
